key_insight: Hallucination risk can be detected directly in intermediate hidden states of LLMs: lightweight residual probes read epistemic signals from question-token representations that are attenuated by final decoding, enabling early, model-agnostic assessment of when a model is likely to hallucinate.
problem_solved: Existing methods detect hallucinations only after fluent (but potentially false) outputs are generated or require expensive external verification. This paper provides a lightweight way to assess hallucination risk from internal activations before or during decoding.
method: Attach small residual probes to intermediate layers to read question-token hidden states and predict per-query/per-token hallucination risk.
Use a training signal linking hidden-state patterns to known hallucination labels (latent testing) so probes learn epistemic uncertainty encoded in intermediate representations.
Operate as a low-overhead, model-agnostic monitoring tool that can be run during inference to flag risky outputs for verification or abstention.
impact: Provides practitioners a practical, low-cost technique to detect and mitigate hallucination risk earlier in the generation pipeline, improving safety, calibration, and routing decisions without modifying the base model.
visual_elements: Schematic of an LLM stack showing probes tapping intermediate residual streams of question tokens and outputting a risk score.
Layer-wise heatmap illustrating where epistemic signals are strongest and how they decay toward final decoding.
Flowchart of deployment: input question → latent probe risk score → decision (accept, verify, abstain).
Bar chart or ROC-style graphic comparing probe-based early detection to output-only hallucination detectors (illustrative)
paper_title: HALT: Hallucination Assessment via Latent Testing
paper_authors: Rohan Bhatnagar, Youran Sun, Chi Andrew Zhang, Yixin Wen, Haizhao Yang
